No, it is not unethical to block ads on a website.

The argument given is that "if we provide interesting content on this website, then when you view the content, you will also view any ads we place alongside the content."

This is a 'covert contract'. You never agreed to watch the ads. You just viewed the website (which they offered freely with no strings attached by putting it up on the internet) and you chose to automatically filter out the parts that you already know you don't want to look at. After the fact, they claim that you're somehow 'stealing' from them by not following the rules that you never agreed to.

They're complaining because you didn't honour their covert contract, but you never signed that contract in the first place and you have no obligation to do so.

I'm not opposed to the idea of Adblock from an ethical perspective--I'm actually using it myself because I'm under some pretty tight bandwidth restrictions at present, and feel that while text-based or image-based ads are not sufficiently obnoxious to justify Adblock, the continued existence of auto-playing video ads, which both distract from the content you were trying to view and soak up bandwidth without your express permission, justifies blocking all ads and then whitelisting based on pledges not to run those ads.

On the other hand, I feel plugins like uBlock, which report to the server that the ads have been viewed, are inherently unethical because they are dishonest. Now instead of viewing a website's content without volunteering to view that website's ads, you are stating to the website that the ads have been viewed, and that misinformation will be passed along to the owners of the ad server, who will make economic decisions based on the lie the uBlock user told. So in the case of a website owner scripting their website to block access to Adblock users, I think the ethical choice to make is to either whitelist the website and deal with the ads, or refuse to view the website at all.
